title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbooks, Benchmarking & Runbooks
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview
--------
This document consolidates the serving runtime reference material for Redwood's serving runtime: runtime architecture, kernel scheduling decisions, profiling playbooks, the canonical benchmarking suite, recent release notes, known issues, and production runbooks. It is intended for engineers (runtime, infra, SRE), solutions engineers onboarding customers to Dedicated/Private, and performance-focused reviewers.

Scope and audience
- Scope: components in the inference serving runtime, scheduler choices used on GPU hosts, profiling and benchmarking methodology, standard runbooks for common incidents.
- Audience: runtime engineers, infra/SRE, oncall engineers, and platform product owners.

Quick links
- Runtime architecture diagram: internal link to diagrams repo (see related_pages).
- Profiling checklist: section below.
- Benchmark harness: ./bench/ directory in serving-runtime repo.

1) Runtime architecture (high-level)
----------------------------------
Intro: Redwood's serving runtime is a layered system that separates request routing, model execution kernel selection, KV/prefix cache management, batching, and telemetry. The design goals are: predictable p99 latency, end-to-end throughput for mixed workloads, graceful degradation under contention, and deterministic cost accounting.

Primary components
- Frontend API (route layer): HTTP/gRPC endpoints, auth, rate limiting, per-customer routing policies.
- Router & policy engine: flow-based routing that chooses destination pool (host, model variant, region) and fallback policy.
- Request broker & batcher: continuous batching loop with per-model/bin queues and latency-aware batching windows.
- Execution worker (GPU process): responsible for kernel selection, KV cache management, GPU memory accounting, and token generation loop.
- Storage & cache: S3-compatible model store, local model cache, NVIDIA NVCache-style model artifacts, and optional shared KV cache for recurrent prefixes.
- Observability pipeline: token-level traces, per-request latency breakdowns, batching metrics, and flamegraphs from profiling collectors.

SLOs and operational targets
- P95 request latency (text-gen, short prompt workloads): <= 120 ms.
- P99 request latency (small models): <= 250 ms.
- Token throughput per GPU (g4-like equivalent, quantized Llama-2-7B): 12k tokens/s sustained for steady-state batched workloads.
- Error rate: < 0.05% 5xx on healthy pools.

Ownership and responsibilities
- Runtime core team: kernel selection, batcher, and execution worker (owner: eng-serving-runtime).
- SRE/Infra: host, GPU fleet, capacity planning, and autoscaling policies.
- Observability/Telemetry: metrics/tracing ingestion and dashboards.

2) Kernel scheduling and placement
----------------------------------
Design goals for scheduling
- Maximize GPU utilization while meeting p99 latency SLOs.
- Minimize context switches and kernel launch overhead.
- Prefer deterministic resource allocation for Dedicated pools.

Scheduling model overview
1. Admission control: requests are classified by priority (realtime, interactive, batch) and by model size. Realtime/interactive get lower queuing tolerance.
2. Per-model bins: work is sharded into bins by sequence-length bucket and model-variant so kernels can be reused and memory footprints are predictable.
3. Batch composition algorithm: continuous window strategy with two levers: time cap (max_wait_ms) and size cap (max_batch_tokens). The batcher applies a cost model to trade latency vs cost.
4. Kernel selector: for each batch the worker chooses between available kernels (fp16, q8_0, q4f16, fused-attention variants) based on target latency and quality profile.

Key configuration knobs (example)
- max_wait_ms = 12  # max time to wait before dispatching a batch (per bin)
- max_batch_tokens = 4096
- kernel_priority = ["fused_attention", "matmul_k_custom", "fallback_cuda"]
- preempt_threshold_ms = 50  # if waiting request is > threshold, preempt a batch for latency-sensitive work

Placement rules
- Dedicated pools: placement is static by GPU-id to ensure cache locality; model artifacts pinned to node local SSD.
- Shared pools (hosted): dynamic placement with affinity scoring (latency history, cache hit rate, cost).

3) Profiling playbook (how to profile a regression)
--------------------------------------------------
When to profile
- New release causes 10%+ regression in p95/p99 latency or throughput.
- New model variant or quantization profile is added.
- Frequent OOMs or unexplained CPU/GPU stalls.

Profiling tools and data sources
- Metrics & traces: Datadog/OTel traces, request-level spans with token timings.
- GPU profiling: Nsight Systems (nsys), Nsight Compute (ncu), and nvprof (for legacy traces).
- Flamegraphs: perf + flamegraph scripts for CPU stacks inside worker process.
- Custom runtime counters: kernel launch latencies, kernel queue depth, kv cache hit/miss.

Step-by-step profiling checklist
1. Reproduce: run the failing workload against a staging pool with identical config. Use the canonical bench harness.
2. Collect traces: enable per-request token timing (10% sampling for live, 100% for staging).
3. GPU capture: run nsys capture for 30-60s during the regression window (nsys profile --output runtime_regression).
4. Inspect kernel timelines: identify long kernels, repeated small kernels, memory copies (H2D/D2H).
5. Check batching distribution: ensure bins are not creating many small batches; inspect batch size histogram.
6. Verify kernel selector: confirm selected kernel variant matches expectation; compare with previous baseline.
7. If needed, run microbenchmarks on suspect kernel with synthetic inputs to determine scalability (vary batch size and sequence length).
8. Document root cause and revert/rollout plan.

Common indicators and remediations
- Symptom: many short-lived kernels with high launch overhead -> increase batch window (max_wait_ms) or bin sizes.
- Symptom: high D2H memcpy overhead -> check memory pinning and prefer zero-copy where supported.
- Symptom: GPU underutilized but high latency -> likely serialization at CPU side (profiling flamegraphs). Increase worker thread pool or move parts to CUDA streams.

Commands and snippets
- nsys: nsys profile -o out.nsys-rep --trace=cuda,osrt --sample=cpu --duration=60 -- python bench/run_workload.py --profile
- ncu (kernel details): ncu --target-processes all -o ncu-report python bench/micro_bench.py
- Flamegraph: perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 30; perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > cpu-flamegraph.svg

4) Benchmarking suite (canonical harness)
----------------------------------------
Benchmark goals
- Representative mixes: short-chat workloads, long-context generation, embeddings, and reranking.
- Reproducible: fixed seeds, controlled host environment, pinned model artifacts.
- Actionable metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/s, GPU SM utilization, memory high-water mark, energy/cost per token.

Bench harness layout
- bench/ (repo) contains: workloads/, runners/, collectors/, and baseline_profiles/.
- Workloads: yaml files describing prompt mixes, sequence length distribution, arrival process (Poisson, steady), and client concurrency.
- Runners: bench runner that can target local GPU, staging pool, or dedicated cluster.
- Collectors: scripts that gather Datadog metrics, nsight captures, and local perf data.

Sample workload config (as text table)
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| workload_name        | arrival_process      | seq_len_dist         |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+
| short-chat-95/5      | Poisson lambda=50    | 95% < 64 tokens      |
| long-gen-4k          | steady 10 clients    | 4k average           |
| embeddings-bulk      | batched 128 inputs   | 128 tokens each      |
+----------------------+----------------------+----------------------+

Benchmark run recommendations
- Use isolated hosts for stable baselines.
- Run each test 3 times and use median for reporting.
- Baseline against previous release artifact stored under baseline_profiles/.

Metrics to capture
- p50/p95/p99 request latency (end-to-end and execution-only).
- tokens/s per GPU and per-host.
- kernel-level latency distribution.
- KV cache hit-rate and model load time.

5) Release notes (latest runtime release: v1.9.0)
-------------------------------------------------
Release date: 2026-02-28
Highlights
- Kernel selector: added fused_attention v2 with 15% p95 improvement on seq_len < 512.
- Batcher: adaptive windowing to reduce small-batch inflation for bursty Poisson arrivals.
- Telemetry: token-level span added and 5x reduction in trace size via compression.
- Bugfix: fixed memory leak in KV cache invalidation path that could cause OOM after ~72h.

Impact & rollout notes
- Default kernel_priority updated; Dedicated pools opted in by default. Hosted pools rolled out canary for 48h before global.

6) Known issues (active)
------------------------
1. Model load time regression (v1.8.x -> v1.9.0)
- Symptom: cold-start model loads increased by ~25% on hosts with high SSD read IOPS.
- Workaround: pre-warm models on node local cache and increase model prefetch concurrency to 4.
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime.

2. Intermittent OOM in q4f16 kernel for 70B-models
- Symptom: out-of-memory during long-context generation with batched requests.
- Workaround: reduce max_batch_tokens for 70B workloads or pin them to nodes with 80GB GPU memory.
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime.

3. Token-skew effect under heavy tail arrivals
- Symptom: small fraction of requests see high token-latency due to unfair batch composition.
- Workaround: enable preempt_threshold_ms=preempt and decrease max_wait_ms for interactive routes.
- Owner: SRE/Infra.

7) Runbooks (incidents and playbooks)
-------------------------------------
A. High p99 latency for interactive routes
1. Check active incidents: run "rg incident runtime" in runbooks index.
2. Inspect route-level dashboards: p99 latency, batch size histogram, preemption events.
3. If small-batch inflation: temporarily increase max_wait_ms by +8 ms for affected bins and monitor.
4. If kernel-level hot path: capture nsys for 30s and escalate to runtime core.
5. Rollback: pin route to fallback model variant (lower memory footprint) and rollback kernel selector to previous baseline if regression started with a recent rollout.

B. OOM on GPU during generation
1. Identify node: run "kubectl -n runtime get pods -o wide | rg OOM" and locate GPU host.
2. Collect logs: /var/log/runtime/worker.log and nsys capture if available.
3. Temporarily evict low-priority batch jobs from that node via scheduler and set node cordon if repeated.
4. Add safety config: max_batch_tokens override for large-model routes.

C. Model cold-start failures
1. Check model store health and local SSD availability.
2. Manual pre-warm: runtimectl prewarm --model-id <id> --node <node-id>
3. If repeated, file for engineering investigation with model store team (attach nfs/iops metrics).

8) Team wiki and contribution guidelines
---------------------------------------
- How to contribute: open a Draft ADR for major scheduler changes; small fixes via PR in the serving-runtime repo. Link to ADR template: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records.
- Performance PR checklist: include benchmark results vs baseline, profiling captures (nsys/ncu), and an ops rollout plan.
- Oncall rotation: runtime oncall is 24/7 with 2-week rotations. Contact escalation chain is in the team roster.

Appendix: useful commands and links
- bench runner: python bench/run.py --workload short-chat-95/5 --target staging --duration 600
- runtimectl: runtimectl status --pool <pool-id> --show-batches
- nsys capture example: nsys profile -o /tmp/trace --sample=cpu -t 60 -- python bench/run.py...
- Dashboards: Datadog -> Dashboards -> Runtime -> Kernel Timelines

If you have additions or corrections, please file a PR against this page and notify the reviewers list.
